I was looking on steam at the games on sale and saw ARK: Survival Evolved and began reading the reviews. What I gathered was that for many players what could have been a fun experience was completely shit on by, for lack of a better word, dickbags. Many would spend hours to progress only to have all their work destroyed in less than a minute.

This is not a problem unique to this game, but seems to be a universal problem to games that have an open world concept and PVP. In GTA Online, aside from the hackers, a frequent source of frustration is high level players killing everyone with their high level weapons/vehicles.

How should game designers in this genre address and rectify this problem?

Here's an idea I had today, feel free to rip it apart:

Dynamic respawn timers.

So a system where players are encouraged not to grief others, and griefers are made targets, in a sense. To elaborate:

Generic sandbox mmo. Players who haven't killed another player respawn instantly, or with a short delay .Player 1 kills someone. Player 1 now has a 5-20 minute respawn timer, so if he dies he has to wait while IN GAME to respawn (no logging out and playing later). It can be strategic to kill another player, and shouldn't be outright banned in this genre, but like in real life, there should be consequences for doing something evil. Players with less time on their respawn timers see those with more time marked with red arrows or something, incentivizing hunting those players down in exchange for reducing their own respawn time total.

Players with no time get nothing from killing a higher timed player, (aside from their equipment which is standard for all deaths, even environmental) so the game focus isn't directed entirely into PVP. Engaging in any form of PVP is a risk/reward system, you could lower your timer from 20 minutes to 5 minutes by killing a target player, or you could die and have wait 20 minutes to continue playing a game. And the kicker: respawn timers NEVER decay. Only by hunting red target players can the timer ever go down. Once you die it's reset to zero and you are once again a "clean" player. And suicides trigger the timer, but cause you to drop all equipment as well.

Edit: and to defend high timer players from further digging their own hole by killing lower players in self defense, the game could have a system where if you are attacked there is no penalty for fighting back.

This is the fault of the game designers. MMO game mechanics should always assume that some percentage of the user base is there to grief, to find the limits of the mechanics and enforced rules, to harvest anything that might be convertable to real world value, and so on. It's an impossible task, or more precisely, an "NP-hard problem", but some games do it much better than others either because they thought harder about the wide variety of ways that they didn't want players to be able to do things, or they had more time to evolve and address problems, or a combination of the two.

I think it's particularly interesting to compare wildly dissimilar games such as Eve Online and Runescape. Griefing is carried to an extreme in Eve Online, even going so far as allowing long cons to steal months or even years of progress from players in an instant and letting it stand when it happens. It's part of the bleak political trust dissonance that pervades the storylines of that game. Runescape, on the other hand, goes so far as to equip every user with a virtual bodycam that can send a report of all recent private chat and surrounding activity to game staff on request. The game's mechanics that deal with attack instigation, location, death, looting, trading, and banking have seen many tweaks over the years to deal with the relentless press of griefers and scammers.

Eve Online and Runescape are examples where what players can do to each other has not only been thought about a lot, but also tuned to the player demographics. Quite a few other MMOs on the other hand, while awesome, are amateurs in terms of deliberate mechanics to enforce fairness of play. In an ideal world, a game's mechanics would be all that would be needed, with everybody understanding and being okay with the idea that if the game allows something to be done, it's not only fair to do, but the game will still generally be fun to play even if a lot of people are doing that. It's not easy to do though, so game designers need to include that consideration when building games, and do the hard work.
